candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: The logical problem of evil fails because neither omnipotence nor perfect goodness entails the hidden premises needed to make God and evil contradictory.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Craig immediately before this uninterrupted opening address, and Grayling is introduced only after it ends.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This extended argument directly contests the alleged logical incompatibility at the heart of the motion and supplies both free-will and morally sufficient-reason defenses.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The traditional atheist claim that an omnipotent, perfectly good God cannot logically coexist with evil.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig reconstructs the logical objection, identifies two unstated assumptions, disputes each, and argues that a possible proposition combining divine existence with permitted evil establishes consistency.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Humans cannot reliably infer that God probably lacks sufficient reasons for evil because their temporal perspective and causal knowledge are severely limited.
candidates.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Craig's continuous opening address and uses the same first-person argumentative framing established after his introduction.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is Craig's first principal answer to the probabilistic problem of evil, challenging the epistemic inference from apparently pointless suffering to divine improbability.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The probabilistic objection that apparently gratuitous evils make the existence of God unlikely.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig shifts from logical consistency to probability and argues that finite observers cannot survey providential history, remote consequences, or the reasons relevant to divine permission of suffering.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Distinctive Christian doctrines make evil less surprising because life's purpose is knowledge of God, suffering may serve that end, and eternal recompense changes its significance.
candidates.attributionBasis: Craig continues without a speaker change, explicitly presenting this material as the second numbered component of his probabilistic response.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move supplies a positive theistic framework under which suffering is compatible with divine purposes, rather than relying solely on human ignorance of those purposes.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The assumption that a loving God's primary purpose would be maximizing happiness during earthly life.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig contrasts happiness-centered expectations with Christian claims about knowing God, entry into an eternal kingdom, and an afterlife whose fulfillment can outweigh severe temporal suffering.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Even if evil lowers the probability of God, rational judgment must consider the full body of evidence, which Craig contends can still make God's existence probable.
candidates.attributionBasis: The numbered transition and uninterrupted delivery identify Craig as the speaker, and the passage closes his opening argument immediately before applause.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This move states Craig's ultimate comparative-evidence answer and supports his concluding claim that neither form of the problem of evil justifies atheism.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The inference from the existence and scale of evil alone to the overall improbability of God's existence.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig argues that probabilities depend on background information, invokes other purported evidence for God, and concludes that evil should not be evaluated in isolation from the total evidential case.

candidates.speaker: A. C. Grayling
candidates.proposition: The tsunami raises a religious-pluralism problem because its victims held many faiths, while Christian exclusivism appears to deny salvation to many who suffered and died.
candidates.attributionBasis: Grayling has just begun the opposing address after Craig's applause, and the moderator's prior introduction plus the uninterrupted first-person delivery fixes attribution.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument connects the debate's signature disaster to competing religious claims and complicates the suggestion that suffering serves a common salvific or greater-good purpose.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's appeal to divine purposes, knowledge of God, and eternal salvation as context for earthly suffering.

candidates.contextSummary: Grayling notes that the disaster killed adherents of diverse religions and no religion, then questions how a proposed greater good relates to incompatible faiths and exclusivist salvation claims.

candidates.speaker: A. C. Grayling
candidates.proposition: If an intelligent supernatural agent is interested in humanity, the world's tsunamis and childhood cancers initially indicate that it is either malevolent or less than omnipotent.
candidates.attributionBasis: This remains Grayling's uninterrupted opposing speech, with first-person transitions linking the argument directly to his preceding tsunami discussion.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The inference from observed suffering to the character or power of a putative deity is Grayling's direct negative answer to whether the relevant form of theistic belief is reasonable.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's conclusion that belief in God remains rational despite natural evil and severe human suffering.

candidates.contextSummary: Grayling conditionally grants a supernatural, active, intelligent, and interested agent, then asks what the observed world implies about it and presents deficient goodness or power as the initial alternatives.

candidates.speaker: A. C. Grayling
candidates.proposition: Craig's defenses create a dilemma: either God lacks the power to prevent suffering in a free world, or God can prevent it but permits it for a proposed greater good.
candidates.attributionBasis: Grayling explicitly refers back to the two points in Craig's presentation while continuing the same uninterrupted opposing address.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This dilemma targets the internal relationship between Craig's free-will defense and greater-good defense, pressing whether they preserve both omnipotence and benevolence together.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's claims that free will limits feasible creation and that benevolence may permit suffering for sufficient reasons.

candidates.contextSummary: Grayling reconstructs Craig's two answers, criticizes cognitive limitation as an unrestricted appeal to mystery, and argues that inability and deliberate permission yield conflicting accounts of divine responsibility.

candidates.speaker: A. C. Grayling
candidates.proposition: Ordinary standards of loving fatherhood make it implausible that a benevolent agent would subject conscious creatures to extreme suffering merely for an unseen greater good.
candidates.attributionBasis: The first-person discussion of fatherhood occurs within Grayling's uninterrupted speech and follows his explicit transition to answering Craig's second point.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The analogy supplies Grayling's substantive moral objection to the greater-good defense by testing divine benevolence against recognizable standards of protective care.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's contention that a perfectly good God may permit terrible suffering to secure morally sufficient overriding ends.

candidates.contextSummary: Grayling grounds expectations about an intelligent, interested deity in human relationships and argues that a caring parent would not impose catastrophic suffering on children for benefits they cannot perceive.

candidates.speaker: A. C. Grayling
candidates.proposition: An omnipotent God should be able to create free creatures in a world with far less suffering, so the claimed necessity of this world's natural evil requires unsupported modal assumptions.
candidates.attributionBasis: Grayling continues the same speech and explicitly turns from the benevolence analogy back to the alleged omnipotence of God.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly attacks the necessity premise behind the free-will and greater-good defenses and extends responsibility across intertwined natural and moral evils.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's claim that God may be unable to actualize a sufficiently good free world containing less evil.

candidates.contextSummary: Grayling proposes worlds with free agency but little or no physical suffering, questions why this quantity of evil is required for good, and argues that divine willing of natural evil implicates related human agency.

candidates.speaker: A. C. Grayling
candidates.proposition: The character of the actual world makes belief in an almighty and all-loving deity unreasonable, especially when supernatural agency already rests on multiple speculative assumptions.
candidates.attributionBasis: This is the concluding stretch of Grayling's uninterrupted address, ending with his explicit negative answer and thanks immediately before applause.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The passage consolidates Grayling's cumulative case and gives his direct answer to the debate question concerning an omnipotent, benevolent deity and the observed world.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's overall defense of the reasonableness of belief in an omnipotent and perfectly loving God despite evil.

candidates.contextSummary: Grayling reviews the speculative path to an interested supernatural being, contrasts world-denying and worldly conceptions of value, emphasizes sentient welfare, and closes by rejecting the reasonableness of the traditional deity.
